questions.question: What enables 'zero-shot cross-lingual transfer' in models like XLM-R?
options: A shared vocabulary and shared representation space across many languages.
Training the model on a translation dictionary for every language.
Running the model through a translator first.
Using a separate model for every language.
questions.explanation: By training on many languages at once with a shared tokenizer, the model learns a language-agnostic space where semantic concepts are linked across languages.

questions.question: Which model set the cross-lingual baseline in 2019 by training on a massive CommonCrawl corpus?
questions.explanation: XLM-RoBERTa (XLM-R) was a major milestone, showing that massive-scale pretraining on 100 languages could produce powerful cross-lingual capabilities.

questions.question: What is the 'fertility tax' for low-resource languages in multilingual models?
options: They are split into many more tokens per word than high-resource languages, increasing cost and latency.
The model charges more per token for these languages.
The model refuses to generate more than 10 words in these languages.
The training data for these languages is more expensive to buy.
questions.explanation: Because tokenizers are often biased toward English/Latin scripts, other languages (like Hindi or Arabic) are broken into much smaller fragments, eating up the context window.

questions.question: Why might fine-tuning on a typologically close language (like Hindi for an Marathi target) be better than English?
options: Language similarity predicts transfer quality better than raw corpus size.
It is always faster to fine-tune on Hindi.
English models are not available for these tasks.
It reduces the number of tokens in the vocabulary.
questions.explanation: Linguistic similarity (shared grammar, scripts, or word roots) often provides a stronger transfer signal than the sheer volume of English training data.
